title: Ontological Paradoxes in the Classification of Oligodendroglia and Other Glia
content: The current categorization of the main cellular elements of the brain was proposed over a century ago by Santiago Ramón y Cajal (neurons, astroglia) and Pío del Río-Hortega (oligodendroglia, microglia). It derives from morphological observations of histochemically stained postmortem human brain and allied inferences about the embryological origins (ectoderm or mesoderm) and specialized functions of each cellular element. The ontology of brain non-neuronal (glial) cells has been broadly substantiated by later research, with astroglia, oligodendroglia and microglia widely viewed as having distinct primary roles relating to metabolic support of neurons, myelination and neuroimmune responses. Yet even early descriptions by Cajal, Hortega and others recognized morphologically distinct subtypes of core neuroglial elements in diverse locations and health states, potentially indicating subtypes with diverse functions. Conversely, modern techniques such as single-cell transcriptomics reveal commonalities in molecular profiles consistent with functional overlap of different core elements, e.g. metabolic support or neuroimmune functions in oligodendroglia. Such non-canonical functions may be linked to pathogenesis in various brain conditions, including neurodegenerative diseases, stroke and brain cancers. We review inconsistencies in prevailing perspectives that may necessitate re-examination of the ontological classification of all neuroglial cell species.
